In7.18.1 C consists of integral k-algebras with flat homomorphisms and F:C→Ens commutes filtered inductive limits. The proof uses F(A→k), but evaluation k[t]→k at t=0 is not flat: tensoring the injective multiplication-by-t map on k[t] gives the zero map on nonzero k. Here is a concrete counterexample on exactly the printed category. Fix algebraically closed k and define G(A)=Z when Frac(A)/k is algebraic and G(A)=0 otherwise. Every flat map of nonzero domains A→B is injective: for nonzero a in A, flatness preserves the injection A --a→ A after tensoring with B; if a mapped to0, the resulting zero map B→B would be injective, forcing B=0. Hence Frac(A) injects into Frac(B), so transcendence over k cannot disappear. Define G on arrows by identity when both values are Z and by the unique map whenever the target is0. There is no arrow from the transcendental case to the algebraic case; these maps compose exactly, so G is a functor. A filtered diagram of these injections has an integral colimit.
